claim: The study integrated single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) data from 727 peripheral and nervous system cell types spanning 17 mouse organs with body mass index (BMI) genome-wide association study (GWAS) data from >457,000 individuals.
source: Here, we integrated recently published single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) data from 727 peripheral and nervous system cell types spanning 17 mouse organs with body mass index (BMI) genome-wide association study (GWAS) data from >457,000 individuals.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of cell types, organs, and individuals analyzed in the study.

claim: 26 exclusively neuronal cell types from the hypothalamus, subthalamus, midbrain, hippocampus, thalamus, cortex, pons, medulla, and pallidum were significantly enriched for BMI heritability (p<1.6×10−4).
source: Developing a novel strategy for integrating scRNA-seq data with GWAS data, we identified 26, exclusively neuronal, cell types from the hypothalamus, subthalamus, midbrain, hippocampus, thalamus, cortex, pons, medulla, pallidum that were significantly enriched for BMI heritability (p<1.6×10−4).
evidence: The abstract reports the number and types of cell types identified as significantly enriched for BMI heritability with a specific p-value threshold.

claim: Midbrain cell types from the anterior pretectal nucleus and periaqueductal gray were replicated using genes harboring coding mutations associated with obesity (p<1.2×10−4).
source: Using genes harboring coding mutations associated with obesity, we replicated midbrain cell types from the anterior pretectal nucleus and periaqueductal gray (p<1.2×10−4).
evidence: The abstract states that specific midbrain cell types were replicated using a different genetic approach with a specific p-value.

claim: Brain nuclei regulating integration of sensory stimuli, learning and memory are likely to play a key role in obesity.
source: Together, our results suggest that brain nuclei regulating integration of sensory stimuli, learning and memory are likely to play a key role in obesity and provide testable hypotheses for mechanistic follow-up studies.
evidence: The abstract concludes with an interpretation of the results suggesting a role for specific brain functions in obesity.

claim: Studies of monogenic obesity syndromes and rodent models have identified melanocortin signaling circuits in the mediobasal and paraventricular hypothalamus as key components in energy homeostasis and obesity.
source: Studies of monogenic obesity syndromes and rodent models of obesity have identified melanocortin signaling circuits in the mediobasal and paraventricular hypothalamus as key components in energy homeostasis and obesity (Morton et al., 2014; Farooqi and O'Rahilly, 2006; Betley et al., 2013).
evidence: The introduction cites previous studies that have identified specific hypothalamic circuits as important for obesity.

claim: Susceptibility to obesity is distributed across numerous brain areas that receive signals from internal sources or external stimuli that act in concert to regulate feeding behavior and energy stores.
source: Yet growing evidence suggests that susceptibility to obesity is distributed across numerous brain areas that receive signals emanating from internal sources (e.g. viscerosensory input from the gastrointestinal tract) or external stimuli (e.g. the sight or smell of food) that act in concert to regulate feeding behavior and energy stores (Grill, 2006; Zeltser, 2018; Grill and Hayes, 2012).
evidence: The introduction cites evidence suggesting that obesity susceptibility involves multiple brain areas.

claim: The identity of brain cell types that drive susceptibility to human obesity remains largely unknown.
source: However, despite an increasing number of genes, cell types and neuronal circuits being implicated in murine energy homeostasis, the identity of brain cell types that drive susceptibility to human obesity remains largely unknown and a systematic assessment of cell types' relevance in obesity is currently lacking.
evidence: The introduction states that the specific brain cell types underlying human obesity susceptibility are not well characterized.

claim: Genome-wide association studies have identified about a thousand common single-nucleotide polymorphisms that associate with body mass index.
source: In recent years, genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified about a thousand common (minor allele frequency, MAF ≥0.1) single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) that associate with body mass index (BMI, defined as weight in kilogram divided by height in meters squared), a heritable and commonly used proxy phenotype for obesity (Locke et al., 2015; Yengo et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites GWAS studies that have identified approximately 1000 SNPs associated with BMI.

claim: The majority of trait-associated SNPs are located in regulatory regions rather than coding regions.
source: In general, the far majority of trait-associated SNPs are located in regulatory regions and hence, unlike coding variants, tagging genetic intervals (or loci) rather than implicating specific genes.
evidence: The introduction states that most GWAS SNPs are in regulatory regions, which is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Genetic variants with rare frequencies are thought to contribute ~50% to the heritability of BMI.
source: Genetic variants with rare frequencies (MAF <0.1) that are typically too low to be captured in GWAS are thought to contribute ~50% to the heritability of BMI (Wainschtein et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites a study estimating the contribution of rare variants to BMI heritability.

claim: Rare variant association studies have identified 14 coding variants across 13 genes in an exome chip analysis across >750,000 individuals.
source: Lately, rare variant association studies have identified 14 coding variants across 13 genes in an exome chip analysis across >750,000 individuals (Turcot et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites a specific rare variant study that identified coding variants associated with obesity.

claim: Most genes identified by rare variant studies, with the exception of MC4R, KSR2 and GIPR, have not previously been implicated in obesity.
source: Interestingly, these genes, with the exception of MC4R, KSR2 and GIPR, have not previously been implicated in obesity, suggesting that key biologic mechanisms underlying obesity have yet to be identified.
evidence: The introduction notes that most genes from rare variant studies are novel obesity genes, citing the Turcot et al. study.

claim: Gene expression data provide an effective scaffold to inform GWAS data for obesity and other traits.
source: Given that a majority of obesity-associated gene variants likely regulate gene expression rather than impact protein function, gene expression data provide an effective scaffold to inform GWAS data for obesity and other traits (Finucane et al., 2015; Calderon et al., 2017; Pers et al., 2015; Hao et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple studies supporting the use of gene expression data to interpret GWAS results.

claim: Genes in BMI GWAS loci are predominantly expressed in the brain.
source: In 2016, we used microarray-based gene expression data to show that genes in BMI GWAS loci are predominantly expressed in the brain (Locke et al., 2015)
evidence: The introduction cites the authors' previous work showing brain enrichment of BMI GWAS genes.

claim: Mouse single-cell RNA-sequencing has been used to implicate mediobasal hypothalamic cell types in obesity.
source: we recently leveraged mouse; single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) to implicate mediobasal hypothalamic cell types in obesity (Campbell et al., 2017).
evidence: The introduction cites a study that used scRNA-seq to identify hypothalamic cell types relevant to obesity.

claim: CELLECT uses a robust continuous representation of cell type expression.
source: Importantly, whereas previous frameworks for genetic prioritization of cell types have either relied on non-polygenic models (Campbell et al., 2017), used binary or discrete representations of cell type expression (Finucane et al., 2015; Skene et al., 2018) or used average expression profiles (Watanabe et al., 2019), CELLECT uses a robust continuous representation of cell type expression.
evidence: The Results section describes a key feature of the CELLECT method that distinguishes it from previous approaches.

claim: CELLEX combines four expression specificity metrics into a single measure (ESμ).
source: Conjointly, CELLEX was built on the observation that different measures of gene expression specificity (ES) provide complementary information and it therefore combines four ES metrics (see Materials and methods) into a single measure (ESμ) representing the score that a gene is specifically expressed in the given cell type (Materials and methods; Figure 1b).
evidence: The Results section describes the CELLEX method and references Figure 1b which illustrates the approach.

claim: ESμ correctly identified known marker genes as being among the most specifically expressed genes in their respective cell types.
source: For both datasets, we computed gene expression specificities for the four metrics and combined them into ESμ across four cell types with known marker genes and found that ESμ correctly identified them as being among the most specifically expressed genes (Figure 1d,e).
evidence: The Results section reports validation of the ESμ metric using known marker genes, with reference to Figure 1d,e.

claim: A median of 2810 specifically expressed genes per cell type were identified in the Tabula Muris dataset.
source: We respectively identified a median of 2810 and 4020 specifically expressed genes per cell type
evidence: The Results section reports the median number of specifically expressed genes identified per cell type in the Tabula Muris dataset.

claim: A median of 4020 specifically expressed genes per cell type were identified in the Mouse Nervous System dataset.
source: We respectively identified a median of 2810 and 4020 specifically expressed genes per cell type
evidence: The Results section reports the median number of specifically expressed genes identified per cell type in the Mouse Nervous System dataset.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of cell types based on ESμ estimates largely reproduced the cell type dendrograms from the original publications.
source: hierarchical clustering of cell types based on the ESμ estimates largely reproduced the cell type dendrograms from the respective original publications (Tabula Muris Consortium et al., 2018; Zeisel et al., 2018), confirming that our ES approach enables cell types profiles to be compared across studies and single-cell protocols (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The Results section reports that clustering based on ESμ reproduced original cell type classifications, with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Two significantly enriched cell types were identified in the Tabula Muris dataset: neurons and oligodendrocyte precursor cells.
source: Applying CELLECT to the 115 – mostly peripheral – cell types, we identified two significantly enriched cell types, namely neurons and oligodendrocyte precursor cells (Bonferroni correction-based false-discovery rate, FDR < 0.05; Figure 2a).
evidence: The Results section reports the identification of two cell types significantly enriched for BMI GWAS signal in the Tabula Muris dataset.

claim: When conditioning on the neuron cell type, the oligodendrocyte precursor cell type was no longer significant.
source: When rerunning CELLECT conditioning on the neuron cell type, the oligodendrocyte precursor cell type was no longer significant, suggesting that we primarily observed a neuronal signal for the BMI GWAS variants.
evidence: The Results section reports a conditional analysis showing that the oligodendrocyte signal depends on the neuronal signal.

claim: CELLECT prioritized etiologically relevant cell types across cognitive, psychiatric, neurological, immunological, lipid and anthropometric traits.
source: In order to verify that our approach, in general, could identify relevant cell types for complex traits, we computed enrichments for nine GWAS including cognitive, psychiatric, neurological, immunological, lipid and anthropometric traits and disorders, and found that CELLECT prioritized etiologically relevant cell types across all six categories (Figure 2b).
evidence: The Results section reports validation of CELLECT across multiple traits, with reference to Figure 2b.

claim: Cortical neurons were prioritized for cognitive traits and psychiatric disorders (educational attainment, intelligence, schizophrenia).
source: Cortical neurons were prioritized for cognitive traits and psychiatric disorders (educational attainment, intelligence, schizophrenia), neuronal cell types for insomnia, immune cells for multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis, growth-related cell types for waist-to-hip ratio (adjusted for BMI) and height, and hepatocytes for low-density lipoprotein levels
evidence: The Results section reports specific cell types prioritized for different trait categories.

claim: Immune cells were prioritized for multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis.
source: Cortical neurons were prioritized for cognitive traits and psychiatric disorders (educational attainment, intelligence, schizophrenia), neuronal cell types for insomnia, immune cells for multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis, growth-related cell types for waist-to-hip ratio (adjusted for BMI) and height, and hepatocytes for low-density lipoprotein levels
evidence: The Results section reports specific cell types prioritized for different trait categories.

claim: Hepatocytes were prioritized for low-density lipoprotein levels.
source: Cortical neurons were prioritized for cognitive traits and psychiatric disorders (educational attainment, intelligence, schizophrenia), neuronal cell types for insomnia, immune cells for multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis, growth-related cell types for waist-to-hip ratio (adjusted for BMI) and height, and hepatocytes for low-density lipoprotein levels
evidence: The Results section reports specific cell types prioritized for different trait categories.

claim: CELLECT had a properly controlled type I error using 1000 null GWAS constructed based on simulated Gaussian phenotypes with no genetic basis.
source: Finally, using 1000 'null GWAS' constructed based simulated Gaussian phenotypes with no genetic basis, we found that CELLECT had a properly controlled type I error and that results were not confounded by the median number of genes and transcripts per cell
evidence: The Results section reports validation of CELLECT using null GWAS simulations.

claim: 22 cell types from eight brain regions were identified as enriched for BMI-associated variants in the Mouse Nervous System dataset.
source: Applying CELLEX and CELLECT on 265 cell types from the across the Mouse Nervous System dataset, we identified 22 enriched cell types annotated to eight brain regions (Figure 3a).
evidence: The Results section reports the identification of 22 BMI-enriched cell types from the Mouse Nervous System dataset.

claim: Sixteen of the 22 BMI GWAS-enriched cell types were also enriched for 'intelligence' and 'worry', two traits genetically anticorrelated with obesity.
source: Sixteen of the 22 cell types were also enriched 'intelligence' and 'worry', two traits genetically anticorrelated with obesity (overlapping sets of associated loci with opposite effect sizes) (Marioni et al., 2016; Nagel et al., 2018).
evidence: The Results section reports overlap between BMI-enriched cell types and cell types enriched for genetically correlated traits.

claim: Non-neuronal (glial and vascular) cells did not exhibit any genetic enrichment for BMI.
source: Similar to previous work, we did not find any enrichment of genetic variants associated with BMI in non-neuronal cell types (Campbell et al., 2017; Watanabe et al., 2019)
evidence: The Results section reports the absence of enrichment in non-neuronal cell types, consistent with previous studies.

claim: No enrichment was detected for a particular type of neurotransmitter type.
source: nor did we detect enrichment for a particular type of neurotransmitter type (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The Results section reports the absence of enrichment for specific neurotransmitter types.

claim: Weighted gene correlation network analysis on expression data from each of the 22 BMI-enriched cell types identified no significant modules.
source: Weighted gene correlation network analysis (WGCNA [Langfelder and Horvath, 2008]) on expression data from each of the 22 BMI-enriched cell types identified no significant modules (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; top associated module, p=1.88×10−4; FDR ≤ 0.1).
evidence: The Results section reports the results of WGCNA analysis on BMI-enriched cell types.

claim: The results were robust to different GWAS sample sizes and inclusion of Metabochip array-based association data.
source: We observed that the results were robust to different GWAS sample sizes and inclusion of Metabochip array-based association data (Yengo et al. and Locke et al.﻿ GWAS Pearson's R = 0.98 and R = 0.83, respectively), and largely invariant to the enrichment methodology used (Pearson's R = 0.82; Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The Results section reports robustness analyses comparing different GWAS datasets and methods.

claim: Another study focused on Parkinson's disease reported BMI GWAS enrichments for the same mouse nervous system cell types with an overlap of 6/10.
source: Finally, during finalizing this work another study focused on Parkinson's disease, reported BMI GWAS enrichments for the same mouse nervous system cell types (overlap; 6/10) (Bryois et al., 2020).
evidence: The Results section cites an independent study that replicated some of the findings.

claim: The 22 BMI GWAS-enriched cell types mapped to eight brain regions: subthalamus, midbrain, hippocampus, thalamus, cortex, pons, medulla and pallidum.
source: The 22 BMI GWAS-enriched cell types mapped to eight brain regions, namely the subthalamus, midbrain, hippocampus, thalamus, cortex, pons, medulla and pallidum (Figure 4a).
evidence: The Results section lists the brain regions to which the enriched cell types map.

claim: None of the other cell types remained significant when conditioning on the top-ranked subthalamic cell type DEINH3.
source: Contrary to our expectations, we found that none of the other cell types remained significant when conditioning on the top-ranked subthalamic cell type DEINH3 (Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The Results section reports conditional analysis results showing that the DEINH3 cell type accounts for much of the enrichment signal.

claim: Four non-overlapping significantly enriched cell populations were identified in the hypothalamus datasets: ARCME−NEURO29, LHA-NEURO20, POA-NEURO21, and POA-NEURO66.
source: We identified four non-overlapping significantly enriched cell populations, namely a ventromedial hypothalamic glutamatergic cell type (ARCME−NEURO29; p=4.9×10−5) expressing Sf1 (ESμ=0.98 and ESμ=0.99) and Cckbr (cholecystokinin B receptor; ESμ=0.98, ESμ=0.95); a glutamatergic cell type from the lateral hypothalamus (LHA-NEURO20; p=4.9×10−5); and two cell types from the preoptic area of the hypothalamus (POA-NEURO21 and POA-NEURO66; p<1.0×10−4; Figure 5).
evidence: The Results section reports the identification of four significantly enriched hypothalamic cell populations.

claim: The ARCME-NEURO29 cell type expresses Sf1 with ESμ values of 0.98 and 0.99.
source: namely a ventromedial hypothalamic glutamatergic cell type (ARCME−NEURO29; p=4.9×10−5) expressing Sf1 (ESμ=0.98 and ESμ=0.99)
evidence: The Results section reports specific expression specificity values for Sf1 in the ARCME-NEURO29 cell type.

claim: The ARCME-NEURO29 cell type expresses Cckbr with ESμ values of 0.98 and 0.95.
source: and Cckbr (cholecystokinin B receptor; ESμ=0.98, ESμ=0.95)
evidence: The Results section reports specific expression specificity values for Cckbr in the ARCME-NEURO29 cell type.

claim: Disrupted leptin signaling in Sf1-expressing ventromedial hypothalamic neurons renders mice more susceptible to diet-induced weight gain.
source: Interestingly, ventromedial hypothalamic neurons have previously been implicated in control of both body fat mass and blood glucose levels; disrupted leptin signaling in Sf1-expressing ventromedial hypothalamic neurons renders mice more susceptible to diet-induced weight gain (Kim et al., 2011)
evidence: The Results section cites a study showing that Sf1 neurons are involved in weight regulation.

claim: Activation of ventromedial hypothalamic Sf1 neurons causes hyperglycemia.
source: and activation of ventromedial hypothalamic Sf1 neurons causes hyperglycemia (Meek et al., 2016).
evidence: The Results section cites a study showing that Sf1 neurons affect glucose regulation.

claim: The ARCME-NEURO29 cell type expresses Bdnf with ESμ values of 0.91 and 0.99.
source: The two cell types also expressed Bdnf (ESμ=0.91, ESμ=0.99)
evidence: The Results section reports specific expression specificity values for Bdnf in enriched cell types.

claim: Mutations in BDNF and its receptor NTRK2 are a known cause of monogenic obesity in humans.
source: mutations in BDNF and its receptor, NTRK2, is a known cause of monogenic obesity in humans
evidence: The Results section states that BDNF and NTRK2 mutations cause monogenic obesity, which is established knowledge.

claim: In mice, BDNF signaling is required for normal energy homeostasis and glucoregulatory control.
source: and, in mice, BDNF signaling is required for normal energy homeostasis and glucoregulatory control (Kamitakahara et al., 2016).
evidence: The Results section cites a study showing the role of BDNF signaling in mouse energy homeostasis.

claim: Clustering of the 347 hypothalamic cell populations based on ESμ values resulted in clusters predominantly separating by cell type rather than by study or single-cell technique.
source: Noteworthy, clustering of the 347 hypothalamic cell populations based on their ESμ values resulted in clusters predominantly separating by cell type rather than by study or single-cell technique, indicating that CELLEX is relatively robust to batch effects (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The Results section reports that clustering based on ESμ groups cell types by biology rather than technical factors.

claim: There was no significant enrichment in neurons expressing the Pomc gene.
source: There was no significant enrichment in neurons expressing the Pomc gene, a neuropeptide-encoding gene with known coding mutations causing monogenic obesity in humans (4/5 of Pomc+ cell populations were nominally enriched; HYPR-NEURO24 (Pomc/Ttr), p=0.002; ARCME-NEURO21 (Pomc/Glipr1), p=0.01; HYPC-NEURO23 (Pomc/Cartp), p=0.03; HYPR-NEURO24 (Pomc), p=3.0×10−3).
evidence: The Results section reports the absence of significant enrichment in Pomc-expressing neurons, despite nominal enrichments.

claim: Pomc expression was detected in each of the three Pomc+ cell populations.
source: By design, Pomc expression was detected in each of the three Pomc+ cell populations
evidence: The Results section reports that Pomc was detected in expected cell populations.

claim: The leptin receptor was detected in agouti-related peptide- and Trh/Cxcl12+ cell populations, two known leptin-sensing cell populations.
source: the leptin receptor was detected in agouti-related peptide- and Trh/Cxcl12+ cell populations, two known leptin-sensing cell populations
evidence: The Results section reports that the leptin receptor was detected in expected cell populations.

claim: Mc4r was only detected and specifically expressed in the Gpr50+ cell population.
source: and, finally, Mc4r was only detected and specifically expressed in the Gpr50+ cell population, which expressed several genes encoding receptors previously related to energy homeostasis (Campbell et al., 2017)
evidence: The Results section reports that Mc4r was specifically expressed in the Gpr50+ cell population.

claim: Among the 23 high-confidence obesity genes, 20 were part of the Arc-ME dataset and 17 of them robustly and specifically expressed in at least one neuronal Arc-ME cell population.
source: Among the 23 high-confidence obesity genes, 20 were part of the Arc-ME dataset and 17 of them robustly and specifically expressed in at least one neuronal Arc-ME cell population (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Figure 5—source data 5).
evidence: The Results section reports the detection of high-confidence obesity genes in Arc-ME cell populations.

claim: Four Arc-ME cell populations were enriched for the high-confidence obesity genes: ARCME-NEURO21, ARCME-OTHER1, ARCME-NEURO32, and ARCME-NEURO28.
source: Moreover, four cell populations were enriched for the high-confidence obesity genes ARCME-NEURO21 (Pomc/Glipr1+), ARCME-OTHER1 (a population of non-Arc-ME neurons potentially from the retrochiasmatic area), ARCME-NEURO32 (Slc17a6/Trhr+; neurons shown to be necessary and sufficient to induce satiety [Fenselau et al., 2017]) and ARCME-NEURO28 (Qrfp+; an orexigenic neuropeptide involved in energy homeostasis [Chartrel et al., 2016]; Bonferroni threshold p<0.05/34; Figure 5b, upper panel).
evidence: The Results section reports four Arc-ME cell populations enriched for high-confidence obesity genes.

claim: A high correlation was observed between the high-confidence obesity gene set- and CELLECT results across the hypothalamus cell types (Pearson's rho = 0.50, p=1.1×10−5).
source: We observed a high correlation between the high-confidence obesity gene set- and CELLECT results across the hypothalamus cell types (Pearson's rho = 0.50, p=1.1×10−5; Figure 5—source data 7).
evidence: The Results section reports a significant correlation between two different approaches to identifying obesity-relevant cell types.

claim: 16 out of the 18 ARCME-detected high-confidence obesity genes increased expression specificity when running CELLEX on all Arc-ME cells compared to ARCME neurons-only.
source: Moreover, we observed that ES values increased with increasing cell population heterogeneity; 16 out of the 18 ARCME-detected high-confidence obesity genes increased expression specificity when running CELLEX on all Arc-ME cells compared to ARCME neurons-only (Figure 5—source data 8).
evidence: The Results section reports that expression specificity increases with cell population heterogeneity.

claim: 22 of the 23 high-confidence obesity genes were among the 25% most specifically expressed genes in at least one cell type across the Tabula Muris, Mouse Nervous System and Arc-ME datasets.
source: Finally, we found that across the Tabula Muris, Mouse Nervous System and Arc-ME datasets, 22 of the 23 high-confidence obesity genes were among the 25% most specifically expressed genes in at least one cell type (Figure 5—source data 9).
evidence: The Results section reports that most high-confidence obesity genes show specific expression in at least one cell type.

claim: The hippocampus and several other brain areas exhibited stronger genetic enrichment signal than the hypothalamus in GTEx RNA-seq data.
source: Finally, to assess whether hypothalamic transcriptional patterns may explain less genetic heritability compared to other brain areas in humans, we applied CELLEX and CELLECT on RNA-seq data from the Genotype-Tissue Expression Consortium and found that the hippocampus and several other brain areas exhibited stronger genetic enrichment signal than the hypothalamus (Figure 5c).
evidence: The Results section reports analysis of human GTEx data showing stronger enrichment in hippocampus than hypothalamus.

claim: The high-confidence obesity genes enriched most strongly for the hypothalamus in GTEx data (p=3.9×10−4, FDR < 0.05).
source: In contrast, the high-confidence obesity genes enriched most strongly for the hypothalamus (p=3.9×10−4, FDR < 0.05; Figure 5—source data 12).
evidence: The Results section reports that high-confidence obesity genes show strongest enrichment in hypothalamus in GTEx data.

claim: Eight significantly enriched cell types were identified using high-confidence obesity genes, of which two replicated cell types from the BMI GWAS analysis: DEGLU5 and MEGLU2.
source: We computed the enrichment of the high-confidence obesity genes within all 265 mouse nervous system cell types and identified eight significantly enriched cell types (one-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test, FDR < 0.05) of which two replicated cell types from the BMI GWAS analysis DEGLU5 and MEGLU2 from the anterior pretectal nucleus and the periaqueductal grey, respectively; p<1.2×10−4.
evidence: The Results section reports replication of two cell types using high-confidence obesity genes.

claim: A significant correlation was observed between the high-confidence obesity genes enrichment- and CELLECT enrichment results (Pearson's R = 0.54, p=3.0×10−21).
source: We observed a significant correlation between the high-confidence obesity genes enrichment- and CELLECT enrichment results (Pearson's R = 0.54, p=3.0×10−21; Figure 5—figure supplement 2a)
evidence: The Results section reports a significant correlation between two different genetic approaches.

claim: The leptin receptor was only specifically expressed in two out of the 22 BMI GWAS-enriched cell types in the Mouse Nervous System dataset: glutamatergic cells from the periaqueductal grey and anterior nucleus of the solitary tract.
source: Interestingly, the leptin receptor, which regulates key energy homeostatic processes in the hypothalamus and when defective may cause syndromic obesity (Choquet and Meyre, 2011) was only specifically expressed in two out of the 22 BMI GWAS-enriched in the Mouse Nervous System dataset cell types, namely glutamatergic cells from the periaqueductal grey and anterior nucleus of the solitary tract (Figure 6a).
evidence: The Results section reports limited expression of the leptin receptor in BMI-enriched cell types.

claim: 17 of the enriched cell types expressed the serotonin receptor 5-Htr2c.
source: By contrast, 17 of the enriched cell types expressed the serotonin receptor 5-Htr2c (5-hydroxytryptamine receptor 2C), a known regulator of energy and glucose homeostasis (Berglund et al., 2013) and a target for anti-obesity pharmacotherapy (Halford et al., 2011; Figure 6b).
evidence: The Results section reports widespread expression of 5-Htr2c in BMI-enriched cell types.

claim: 5-Htr2c was most specifically expressed in the anterior pretectal nucleus (DEGLU5, ESμ=0.96).
source: 5-Htr2c was most specifically expressed in the anterior pretectal nucleus (DEGLU5, ESμ=0.96), the cell type among our results which most specifically expressed Pomc (ESμ=0.41).
evidence: The Results section reports the highest expression specificity of 5-Htr2c in the DEGLU5 cell type.

claim: Mice lacking the Htr2c in Pomc neurons are resistant to 5-Htr2c agonist Lorcaserin-induced weight loss.
source: Mice lacking the Htr2c in Pomc neurons are resistant to 5-Htr2c agonist Lorcaserin-induced weight loss (Berglund et al., 2013)
evidence: The Results section cites a study showing the role of 5-Htr2c in Pomc neurons for weight loss.

claim: Susceptibility to obesity conferred by common variants is distributed across a mosaic of neuronal cell types, a majority of which are involved in regulating integration of sensory stimuli, learning and memory.
source: Together our results indicate that susceptibility to obesity conferred by common variants, while enriching for some hypothalamic cell types such as VMH Sf1-expressing neurons, is distributed across a mosaic of neuronal cell types of which a majority is involved in regulating integration of sensory stimuli, learning and memory.
evidence: The Results section concludes with an interpretation of the overall findings.

claim: The inferior colliculus and medial geniculate nucleus process auditory input.
source: The inferior colliculus (implicated by MEGLU7, MEGLU10 and MEGLU11) and medial geniculate nucleus (MEINH3) process auditory input
evidence: The Discussion section describes the known functions of brain regions implicated by the enriched cell types.

claim: The superior colliculus is involved in translation of visual input into directed behavior.
source: the superior colliculus for translation of visual input into directed behavior (MEGLU1 and MEGLU6)
evidence: The Discussion section describes the known functions of brain regions implicated by the enriched cell types.

claim: The anterior pretectal nucleus processes somatosensory input.
source: the anterior pretectal nucleus processes somatosensory input (DEGLU5 and MEINH4)
evidence: The Discussion section describes the known functions of brain regions implicated by the enriched cell types.

claim: The piriform cortex and anterior olfactory nucleus process odor perception.
source: and the piriform cortex (TEGLU17) and anterior olfactory nucleus (TEGLU19) processing odor perception.
evidence: The Discussion section describes the known functions of brain regions implicated by the enriched cell types.

claim: The superior colliculus and anterior pretectal nucleus have been implicated in predatory behavior.
source: The superior colliculus and anterior pretectal nucleus have both been implicated in predatory behavior (Shang et al., 2019; Antinucci et al., 2019)
evidence: The Discussion section cites studies implicating these brain regions in predatory behavior.

claim: The superior colliculus and anterior pretectal nucleus project to the zona incerta.
source: and project to the zona incerta, a less well-described brain area situated between the thalamus and hypothalamus that receives direct input from mediobasal hypothalamic Pomc neurons (Wei et al., 2018).
evidence: The Discussion section cites a study describing projections to the zona incerta.

claim: In rats, lesioning of the zona incerta impairs feeding responses.
source: In rats, lesioning of the zona incerta impairs feeding responses (Stamoutsos et al., 1979)
evidence: The Discussion section cites a study showing the role of zona incerta in feeding.

claim: In mouse models, optogenetic stimulation of GABAergic neurons in the zona incerta leads to rapid, binge-like eating and body weight gain.
source: while, conversely, in mouse models, optogenetic stimulation of GABAergic neurons in the zona incerta leads to rapid, binge-like eating and body weight gain (Zhang and van den Pol, 2017).
evidence: The Discussion section cites a study showing the role of zona incerta neurons in feeding behavior.

claim: Activation of projections from the hypothalamic preoptic nucleus to the ventral periaqueductal gray induces object craving.
source: Activation of projections from the hypothalamic preoptic nucleus (DEINH5; POA-NEURO21, POA-NEURO66) to the ventral periaqueductal gray (MEGLU2 and MBDOP1) induce object craving (Park et al., 2018)
evidence: The Discussion section cites a study showing the role of these projections in craving behavior.

claim: Pharmacological inactivation of the periaqueductal gray decreases food consumption.
source: whereas pharmacological inactivation of the periaqueductal gray decreases food consumption (Tryon and Mizumori, 2018).
evidence: The Discussion section cites a study showing the role of periaqueductal gray in food consumption.

claim: Feeding is not an unconditioned response to an energy deficiency but rather reflecting behavior conditioned by learning and experience.
source: Feeding is not an unconditioned response to an energy deficiency but rather reflecting behavior conditioned by learning and experience (Woods and Begg, 2015).
